Meat / Restaurant

Chadolbaegi with Scallion-Soy Dipping Sauce

Chadolbaegi — paper-thin frozen beef brisket shavings — is the tabletop grill's speed round.

Korean · Easy · Serves 4

Jump to recipe ↓
Chapter 01 / 20 meat recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: restaurant. Chadolbaegi — paper-thin frozen beef brisket shavings — is the tabletop grill's speed round. The slices are cut while frozen hard, dropped on the grate still frost-cold, and cooked in seconds per side; the whole pleasure is the contrast of a crisp lacy edge against a melting, barely-set center, dunked in a sharp scallion-soy dip. It is the cheapest cut on the K-BBQ menu and routinely the favorite order, because chadolbaegi's ratio of drama to effort has no rival. Ten seconds of patience at the fire, and the fat does everything else.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Keep the meat frozen until the moment it grills. This is the one record where "straight from the freezer" is the technique: thawed chadolbaegi welds to the grate and loses the shavings' shape. Work from the freezer in batches.
  • Mix the dip in a bowl the whole table can reach: everything whisked, scallions last. It should taste sharp and a little hot — the meat is rich and needs a dip that fights back.
  • Set the grill to its hottest sustainable setting; chadolbaegi wants the same fire you'd sear a steak on, about 230 °C at the grate if you can measure.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Lay the frozen shavings flat, one layer, as many as fit without touching. They cook in 8–12 seconds a side — the grill boss stands over them with tongs the entire time. The edge will crisp and frill while the center barely sets; that is the dish. Checkpoint — the color change runs pink-frost to gray-brown at the edges with the fat turning translucent. Pull the slice the moment it no longer looks raw; a fully cooked-through chadolbaegi slice is a ruined one.
  2. 02
    Dip while hot, straight from tongs to bowl to mouth. Rice between rounds; the fat is rich in a way that wants starch and acid beside it. Checkpoint — eating test: crisp edge, melting center, the dip's vinegar and scallion cutting the fattiness. If it tastes purely of fat, the dip is too gentle — more vinegar and gochugaru.
  3. 03
    Repeat in small batches. The shavings come off the freezer pack a handful at a time; any that thaw on the platter go on the grill immediately at a slightly cooler spot, or into the next round of fried rice instead. Checkpoint — by the last batch the dip bowl should be reduced and cloudy from repeated dunking — the traditional end state, and the sign of a full table. Chef’s Note — the brisket point's fat marbling is why the frozen shave works at all: the fat protects the slice through the hard sear and then melts at the table. That is also why substitutions fail — lean eye of round shaved the same way turns to gray paper in the same ten seconds. If you cannot get brisket, use well-marbled chuck and call it what it is; the technique carries, the name does not.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Slices weld to the grateGrate not hot enough or meat thawedPreheat harder; work from frozen
Slices gray and overcookedPulled late8–12 seconds a side; pull at no-raw-look
Greasy aftertasteDip too mildMore vinegar, more scallion, more gochugaru
Thawed shavings stuck togetherSat out between batchesFreezer until each batch; separate while still frost-hard

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • The frozen block keeps 2 months sealed; thawed slices should be cooked the same day. The dip keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves overnight.
  • Variations: the dip builds toward cho-gochujang (#SA03) for a hotter table; leftover shavings into kimchi fried rice; the same dip on grilled mushrooms (#SF02's lane) carries the vegan table.
